opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think of it as a straight line from Reachy Mini to a humanoid, where you just keep adding motors until you get a person. The small robots taught us something more important: the bottleneck isn't really the hardware. It's the community, the software, and the data.

When we put out Reachy Mini, the goal was to get robots onto people's desks. That means students, hobbyists, and researchers who would never have touched a robot because it cost tens of thousands of dollars and needed a lab. Once you have thousands of people tinkering, writing apps, sharing behaviors, and contributing datasets, you've built the thing that's actually missing in robotics. That's an open ecosystem, very similar to what happened with language models on the Hub.

So the humanoid path, for us, is about scaling that ecosystem up step by step. You go from a small expressive robot, which is mostly about interaction, perception, and personality, to something with arms that can manipulate objects. Then you add mobility. Each step reuses the same open software stack and the same way of sharing models and data. That's what something like LeRobot is for. You don't want every new form factor to start from zero.

I'll also say I'm a bit contrarian about humanoids as the default. The humanoid form makes sense because our world is built for human bodies, but a lot of useful work doesn't need legs, and legs are expensive and hard to make safe. I think we'll see a lot of intermediate forms first: wheeled bases with arms, tabletop robots, specialized helpers. Full humanoids will come, but I'd rather they arrive with open designs and open models, so no single company owns what's essentially going to be a new kind of computer in people's homes.

So the progression is less "small robot, then big robot" and more "build the open community and tooling at a price point people can afford, then let the form factors grow on top of that." If we get the openness right at the small scale, the humanoid becomes a natural extension rather than a moonshot.

r001.rationale: The response describes growing an open robotics community through small, affordable robots, then scaling that shared ecosystem and tooling as robot form factors progress toward humanoids.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way we think about it is really as a ladder, and Reachy Mini is the first rung. The whole point of Mini was to get something cheap enough, like a few hundred dollars, that a lot of people could actually have one on their desk and start hacking on it. Because the thing we learned with the models is that the community moves way faster than any single lab once you give them something they can run at home. We wanted the same dynamic for robotics.

The next step up is Reachy 2, which Pollen had already built before they joined us. That's a full-size robot with two arms, a mobile base, the head with the antennas. It's much more expensive, obviously, so it's more for labs and companies, but it's already the platform where we and a bunch of others are collecting teleoperation data and training policies with LeRobot. So you already have this continuity, the same software stack running from the tiny thing on your desk up to the big one.

And then humanoid. Honestly, I don't think we need to be the ones building the hardware for a full humanoid right away. There are already a lot of companies doing that, some of them very well. What we care about is the open side, the software, the datasets, the models. If the policies you train on a Reachy or even on a SO-100 arm can transfer, and we're seeing early signs that cross-embodiment training actually works, then the form factor becomes almost a detail. You'd want the open-source humanoid at some point, sure, the same way we eventually wanted open models at every size. But the sequence for us is community first, data second, and bigger bodies come as the data and the models justify them.

The other thing I'd say is that I'm not convinced the humanoid is the end point in the way people assume. A robot in a home doesn't necessarily need legs. It might need to be small, safe, kind of cute, something you don't mind having around your kids. Reachy Mini is partly an experiment on that question too. So we'll go up the ladder, but I'd like to keep an open mind on what the top of the ladder actually looks like.

r001.rationale: The response describes a progression from Reachy Mini to larger robots and says the sequence is “community first,” with an affordable Mini that lets people start hacking on robotics.

astra-6.text:
I think the progression is really through the software and the learning, rather than just making the robot bigger. With Reachy Mini, you have something accessible that people can put on their desk, experiment with, and build applications for. That lets a much broader community explore what a robot should do and how it should interact with us.

A humanoid adds a lot of complexity: manipulation, balance, safety. So I wouldn’t see it as simply scaling up Reachy Mini. The idea is to build an open ecosystem where the models, the datasets, and the things people learn can transfer across different robots. Humanoids can be one destination, but we should let useful applications guide the form factor.

r001.rationale: The response says accessible small robots let a broader community experiment and build applications, and proposes an open ecosystem where what people learn transfers across robots, including humanoids.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is what we can learn with a small robot that will transfer to a bigger one. With Reachy Mini, you can already explore perception, interaction, and how a robot behaves around people. You can put it in the hands of many more developers, and they can try things we wouldn’t have thought of ourselves.

But I wouldn’t describe it as simply scaling up Reachy Mini until you have a humanoid. Walking, balance, manipulating objects safely—those bring very different challenges. What I’d like to see is a shared, open ecosystem where people working on different bodies can build on each other’s software, models, and data. Then the humanoid becomes one form factor in that ecosystem. You choose the body for what you want the robot to do.

r001.rationale: The response proposes involving many developers and building a shared, open ecosystem so people working on different robot bodies can build on one another’s work as humanoids emerge.
